script.title: Why Edison Added a Carbon Button

lines: Thomas Edison bit the wood of his piano to hear it.
He had hearing loss.
Biting let him hear through his teeth and jaw.
In March 1876, Alexander Graham Bell sent a spoken sentence through a liquid transmitter, the part you speak into.
Some phones with liquid transmitters soon went out of use.
Then, on 27 April 1877, Edison filed a patent for a carbon transmitter.
Inside, grains of carbon sat between two metal plates.
One plate was very thin and faced the speaker.
Sound shook that plate, and the plate pressed the grains.
Pressed grains sat closer together, so electricity passed through more easily.
A steady current ran through them.
As the pressure changed, the current changed too, copying the sound.
You see, it's like squeezing a handful of loose sand.
The grains press together and touch more.
Those carbon transmitters were much louder than the other kinds.
Edison and Emile Berliner fought a long court battle over who invented it.
In 1892, a federal court ruled Edison was the inventor.
Carbon microphones were widely used in telephones until the 1980s.
So a man who bit his piano to hear it helped make phones louder.
He even suggested the word people still use to answer a call: hello.

claims.claim: Edison bit the wood of his piano and his phonograph to hear through his teeth and jaw, and his hearing loss shaped how he listened.
On 10 March 1876 Bell transmitted a sentence using a liquid transmitter and an electromagnetic receiver; some early telephones used liquid transmitters, which soon went out of use.
On 27 April 1877 Edison filed for a patent on a carbon (graphite) transmitter.

A carbon microphone has two metal plates separated by granules of carbon; one plate is very thin and faces the speaker as a diaphragm; sound makes it vibrate and press the granules, changing resistance; higher pressure lowers resistance as granules are pushed closer; a steady direct current through the granules is varied to reproduce the sound.
Most early telephones used Edison/Berliner carbon transmitters, which were much louder than the other kinds.
Edison and Berliner fought a long legal battle; a federal court ruled in 1892 that Edison, not Berliner, was the inventor of the carbon microphone.
Carbon microphones were widely used in telephones until the 1980s.
Thomas Alva Edison suggested the word Hello for answering the telephone, still used today.
